title: Abijam and Asa of Judah; Nadab and Baasha of Israel
summary: Abijam reigns briefly in Judah and follows his father's sins, but God keeps a lamp for David. His son Asa reigns forty-one years, removes idols and even deposes the queen mother, yet buys an alliance with Aram to stop Baasha of Israel. In the north, Jeroboam's son Nadab is assassinated by Baasha, who wipes out Jeroboam's house as Ahijah foretold and then continues in Jeroboam's sin.
story: The narrative now settles into the rhythm that carries the rest of Kings: reign after reign, alternating between Judah and Israel, each dated by the other kingdom's king and judged by a theological standard. Judah's kings are measured against David; Israel's against Jeroboam. This chapter shows both measures at work. In Judah the promise to David holds the line steady even through a bad king, and Asa brings the first reform since the division. In Israel, Ahijah's word against Jeroboam's house (14:10) is fulfilled within two years of his death, and the first of the northern kingdom's many coups begins a pattern of violent turnover that will mark its whole history.
historical:
Abijam reigned about 913 to 911 BC and Asa about 911 to 870 BC; Nadab's short reign fell about 910 to 909, and Baasha's about 909 to 886. Such dates are approximate, and the chronology of the kings is complicated by overlapping reigns and different ways of counting a king's first year, which scholars such as Edwin Thiele have tried to reconstruct. The formula dating a king of one kingdom by the regnal year of the other (verses 1, 9, 25, 28, 33) is how the book ties the two histories together.

The war between Asa and Baasha centered on the border just north of Jerusalem. Ramah lay about five miles north of the city on the main road, so fortifying it choked Judah's access north. Asa's response was to pay Ben-hadad of Damascus, grandson of Hezion (possibly the Rezon of 11:23, though that identification is uncertain), to break his treaty with Israel and attack its northern towns. Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, and Chinnereth (near the Sea of Galilee) were on Israel's northern frontier. Gibbethon, where Nadab was killed, was a Philistine town on the western edge of Israel's territory, fought over for decades (16:15).
cultural:
The queen mother (verse 13) held an official position at the Judean court, and her name is recorded for nearly every king of Judah. Removing Maacah from it was a public political act, not only a family quarrel. The Hebrew of verses 2 and 10 calls her the mother of both Abijam and Asa; the BSB, like many translations, takes her as Asa's grandmother, since mother can mean ancestress in Hebrew, and she evidently kept her status into a second reign. Her Asherah image was burned in the Kidron Valley, east of the city, which became the usual place to destroy idolatrous objects.

Treaties in the ancient Near East were sworn between kings and often described as passing from father to son (verse 19). Asa's gift of silver and gold is called in Hebrew by a word that often means a bribe. The high places (verse 14) were local hilltop shrines, some devoted to the LORD and some to other gods; even kings who were praised often left them standing, and Kings notes this each time until Hezekiah and Josiah finally remove them.
literary: The chapter is built from four regnal accounts, two for Judah (verses 1-8, 9-24) and two for Israel (verses 25-32, 33-34), each framed by the standard formulas: when the king began, how long he reigned, how he is judged, a source reference, and his death and successor. The judgments are the heart of each account. Abijam's heart was not fully devoted (verse 3), while Asa's heart was fully devoted all his days (verse 14), using the same Hebrew word. Nadab and Baasha both walked in the way of Jeroboam. Refrains carry the theme: there was war between the kings (verses 6, 7, 16, 32), and the reign of each northern king is tied to the sin which Jeroboam had caused Israel to commit.

outline.t: Abijam of Judah and the lamp kept for David
War with Baasha and the alliance with Aram
Nadab of Israel and the end of Jeroboam's house

doctrines.note: Abijam deserved to lose the throne, but for the sake of David the LORD gave him a lamp in Jerusalem (verse 4). God's covenant with David, not the merit of each king, preserves Judah's royal line.
Asa's reforms show repentance as concrete action: idols removed, cult prostitution banished, even his own grandmother deposed for idolatry. Reform cost him family peace and political comfort.

Asa's heart was devoted, yet in a crisis he emptied the temple treasury to buy a foreign king's help. The chapter shows a real believer relying on political means rather than on God, a lapse 2 Chronicles 16:7-9 records a prophet rebuking.

words.note: Yashar, upright or right. To do what was right in the eyes of the LORD (verses 5 and 11) is the book's highest verdict on a king. The word pictures a straight path, conduct that matches God's standard rather than the king's own.

Berit, covenant or treaty. Used twice in verse 19 for alliances between kings. The same word names God's covenant with Israel, which gives Asa's political treaty an irony: he trusted one kind of covenant in a moment when the other should have been enough.

Shochad, a gift or bribe. The word usually describes payment that corrupts judgment. Here it names Asa's payment to Ben-hadad, a hint that the narrator does not simply approve the deal, even though it worked.

christ: The lamp that God keeps burning for David through unworthy kings is one of the Old Testament's steady signs that the promise of 2 Samuel 7 will not fail. The New Testament traces Jesus' genealogy through these very kings, including Abijam (Abijah) and Asa (Matthew 1:7), showing that the promise passed through flawed hands to reach its fulfillment. The pattern of the northern kingdom, where one dynasty after another is overthrown in blood, shows what happens when power is seized rather than received, the opposite of the kingdom Jesus announces, which comes as a gift from the Father. These links are covenantal and thematic, not predictions within the chapter.

hard.q: Asa's heart was fully devoted to the LORD, yet he paid a pagan king to attack Israel. Does the text approve of what he did?
hard.a: Kings reports the alliance without an explicit verdict, and it succeeded: Baasha withdrew. But the narrator's details lean critical. Asa emptied the temple treasury that he had just filled (verse 15), paid what the Hebrew calls a bribe, and invited a foreign power to attack fellow Israelites, opening a door Aram would use against both kingdoms for generations. The parallel account in 2 Chronicles 16 is explicit: the prophet Hanani rebukes Asa for relying on the king of Aram instead of the LORD. Readers differ on how to weigh this against the praise of verse 14. Most conclude that the book's verdict on Asa's heart describes his lifelong loyalty to the LORD against idols, while this episode shows that loyal kings could still fail to trust God in a crisis.

questions: Asa removed his own grandmother from her position for her idolatry. When does faithfulness to God require costly decisions within a family?
Asa's plan worked, yet it was not an act of trust. How do you tell the difference between wise action and relying on yourself instead of God?
God kept a lamp burning for David through kings who did not deserve it. How does that shape the way you think about God's faithfulness to you?
